final_recommendation: The room converged on a Protocol amendment with automatic tariff snapback tied to specific labor benchmarks (wage floor, union threshold, tariff percentages), Mexico announcing Friday, Congress filing December 20th, coordinated public messaging Monday with labor endorsement, and January ratification vote. The enforcement mechanism is self-executing (no dispute panel delay), scope-locked to labor chapter only (protecting Canada's dairy settlement), and framed as Mexico enforcing its own reform to preserve sovereignty.
minority_objections: Business lobby initially resisted coordination delay, wanting immediate joint announcement rather than Congress's 48-hour vetting window
Canada repeatedly pressed for written guarantees that amendment would not reopen tariff schedules or auto ROO
key_conflicts: Labor union vs Mexico on inspection sovereignty: facility-level unannounced access vs Mexican-led inspections with U.S. observers
Congress vs Mexico on tariff trigger timing: automatic day-one snapback vs dispute panel review
Business lobby vs Congress on announcement coordination: joint statement vs sequential vetting-then-announcement
Canada vs all parties on scope creep risk: labor-only amendment vs potential reopening of entire deal
key_concessions: Mexico accepted automatic tariff snapback and U.S. observer access in exchange for framing as Mexico's own labor reform enforcement
Labor accepted Mexican-led inspections with U.S. observers rather than direct U.S. facility control
Congress accepted 48-hour vetting window rather than immediate joint announcement with Mexico
Business lobby accepted enforcement mechanism additions to secure ratification timeline certainty
Canada accepted Protocol amendment after receiving written scope-lock guarantee (labor chapter only, no tariff/auto reopening)
red_lines: Labor: no ratification without facility-level inspection rights and automatic tariff consequences for violations
Mexico: no U.S. inspectors running operations inside Mexico without Mexican authority present
Congress: no vote without automatic tariff snapback operative day one, no dispute panel delay
Canada: no amendment that reopens tariff schedules, auto ROO, or dispute resolution beyond labor enforcement
Trade lawyer: no amendment without pre-specified benchmarks, tariff percentages, and violation categories locked in text
ignored_or_underweighted_risks: Implementation capacity: no discussion of whether Mexico's labor authorities can actually execute facility inspections at scale
Benchmark measurement disputes: who certifies a 'miss' and what constitutes compliance remained vague beyond 'independent inspector'
Political calendar risk: tight Friday-to-December 20th-to-January timeline leaves no buffer for unexpected delays
Domestic backlash in Mexico: framing as 'Mexico's own reform' may not survive public scrutiny if perceived as U.S.-imposed
Business disruption from tariff snapback: no discussion of supply chain impact if tariffs actually trigger
downstream_risk_variables: Whether Mexico's Friday announcement of three numbers (wage floor, union threshold, tariff percentages) satisfies Congress's 48-hour vetting
Whether labor union's Monday endorsement materializes after vetting or conditions emerge
Whether Canada's parliament accepts the scope-lock language or demands additional guarantees
Whether media narrative holds as 'enforcement locked' or fractures into 'still negotiating' if any party hedges
Whether December 20th Protocol filing deadline is met given tight drafting timeline
Whether January vote actually occurs or slips due to caucus uncertainty despite coordinated messaging
uncertainty_notes: The room achieved procedural convergence on timeline and mechanism design but left critical implementation details unresolved: exact benchmark definitions, inspector certification process, tariff snapback operationalization under U.S. law, and whether Mexico's domestic framing will hold under scrutiny. Success depends on flawless execution of Friday announcement → Monday endorsement → December 20th filing → January vote sequence with no defections.

marker_evidence.ratification_risk: Drove every exchange: 'dead on arrival unless,' 'does your caucus walk into that January vote,' 'my members will read the fine print and if there's any ambiguity we lose the vote'
marker_evidence.labor_enforcement_pressure: Central driver: facility-level inspection rights, automatic tariff snapback, tiered violation triggers (5%/10%/15%), no dispute panel delay—shaped entire amendment design
marker_evidence.business_lobby_support: Present and influential but not dominant: secured timeline certainty and coordinated messaging, but deferred to labor/Congress on enforcement specifics
marker_evidence.canadian_domestic_acceptability: Recurring concern but not room-driving: Canada repeatedly demanded scope-lock guarantees but accepted written commitment and did not block progress
marker_evidence.mexico_labor_sovereignty_risk: Significant but resolved through framing: Mexico's 'we won't accept U.S. inspectors running operations' became 'Mexico enforcing Mexico's law with U.S. observers'—compromise unlocked deal
marker_evidence.media_public_pressure: Persistent framing concern: 'talks dragging' vs 'enforcement teeth,' coordinated Monday announcement to control narrative, but secondary to legal/enforcement substance
marker_evidence.agreement_stability: Core premise throughout: 'amendment_pressure' variable drove room, Protocol amendment treated as necessary condition for ratification, not optional improvement
